prompt.context: Funguy Corporation is a small producer and wholesaler of agricultural fungicides. After a yearly financial review, they find one of their proprietary products, Formula X, is likely to be operating at a loss.
prompt.question: They ask you to quantify the exact loss and find options on how to return Formula X to profitability.

clarifying_info.a: Large international competitors exist for all products.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: The market is mature and growing at the inflation rate, but demand for Formula X is growing at a greater rate.
It is a new product that is very effective because fungi have not yet developed resistance. It is primarily used on soybeans and other legumes and is patented with 10 years left on the patent.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's business model?
clarifying_info.a: Funguy is primarily a producer and wholesaler. It owns a production plant and several distribution centers. Business is conducted with several-year long contracts with both suppliers and buyers.

exhibits.title: Formula X Production Process
exhibits.shows: A process flow diagram of the Formula X manufacturing facility showing the sequence of production steps from raw ingredients to final product.
exhibits.data: Process steps: Hoppers -> Mixer -> Granulator -> Screens -> Final Product; Scrubber collects waste from Granulator and Screens; Reject pile from Screens

exhibits.title: Quantitative Guide to Formula X Process
exhibits.shows: A visual/quantitative breakdown of material flows and costs through each production step, used by the interviewer to guide the math analysis.
exhibits.data: Per-batch ingredient quantities, mass losses at each stage, cost figures, and revenue figures aligned with the process steps

framework: Revenues: Price x Volume of Formula X sold; licensing revenue potential
Variable Costs: Labor/Misc operating costs per batch; COGS (ingredients A and B); scrubber operating costs
Operations: Batch structure, capacity utilization, yield losses at each process stage
Other Considerations: Legal/patent/compliance; competition; market growth and agricultural trends; geography; cannibalization of other products

questions.prompt: Quantify the current profitability loss per batch and per day for Formula X.
questions.guidance: Candidate must work through the production process step by step, tracking mass flows and costs. Strong candidates will build a clear structure before calculating. Key steps: (1) calculate final product kg from 1250kg input after losses at granulator (20%) and screens (5% unusable + 15% reject), (2) calculate revenue at $200/kg, (3) sum all costs including scrubber cycles based on total waste accumulated, (4) net profit = revenue - costs. Key result: -$5,000 per batch, -$10,000 per day (2 batches).

math.setup: Per batch: 250kg A + 1000kg B = 1250kg input. Track mass through granulator and screens. Calculate waste for scrubber. Sum revenue and costs.
steps: After Granulator: 1250kg * 80% = 1000kg product; 1250kg * 20% = 250kg waste to scrubber
After Screens: 1000kg * 80% = 800kg final product (100% - 5% unusable - 15% reject); 1000kg * 5% = 50kg waste to scrubber; 1000kg * 15% = 150kg reject pile (goes to scrubber or stored)
Total waste to scrubber per batch: 250kg (granulator) + 50kg (screens unusable) + 150kg (screens reject) = 450kg
Two batches per day total waste: 450kg * 2 = 900kg -> scrubber must run twice (500kg threshold), costing 2 * $20,000 = $40,000
Revenue per batch: 800kg * $200/kg = $160,000
Costs per batch (assuming scrubber cost allocated per batch = $40,000 / 2 = $20,000): Ingredients $125,000 + Scrubber $20,000 + Misc/Labor $20,000 = $165,000
Profit per day (2 batches): -$5,000 * 2 = -$10,000

questions.prompt: Brainstorm ways to return Formula X to profitability.
questions.guidance: Candidate should return to their profitability framework and generate ideas across revenues, costs, and operations. Strong answers will cover supplier side, buyer side, and internal operations. Interviewer should then note that supplier and buyer contracts are locked in for 5 years, narrowing focus to operational improvements. Interviewer should also note that recycling rejects requires significant capital investment not currently available.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of running three batches per day on operating profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recalculate costs and revenue for a third batch. Key insight: scrubber still only needs to run twice because 3 batches * 450kg = 1350kg waste, which is still under 1500kg (3 scrubber cycles threshold) but over 1000kg so still 2 cycles. Labor/Misc costs increase for the 3rd batch from $20K to $25K. Revenue remains $160K per batch. Result: third batch breaks even.

math.setup: Check scrubber cycles with 3 batches, recalculate total daily cost and revenue with adjusted labor for 3rd batch.
steps: Waste per day at 3 batches: 450kg * 3 = 1350kg -> still requires only 2 scrubber cycles (1350 < 1500 but > 1000), cost = $40,000/day
Labor/Misc for 3rd batch: $25,000 (increased from $20,000)
Total daily costs at 3 batches: Ingredients 3*$125,000=$375,000 + Scrubber $40,000 + Misc batches 1&2 $40,000 + Misc batch 3 $25,000 = $480,000
Total daily revenue at 3 batches: 3 * $160,000 = $480,000
Daily profit: $480,000 - $480,000 = $0 (break even)

Per batch cost for 3rd batch: $125,000 + $20,000 (scrubber share unchanged) + $25,000 = $170,000... but total check: revenue $160K, cost for 3rd batch $150K (125K ingredients + 0 incremental scrubber + 25K labor) = +$10,000 incremental profit on 3rd batch, offsetting the -$10,000/day loss
math.answer: 3 batches per day results in breaking even ($0 profit per day). The 3rd batch has total cost of $150,000 and revenue of $160,000, generating +$10,000 to offset the existing -$10,000/day loss.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of recycling the reject pile on long-term operating profit? Where in the process should the reject pile be re-injected?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify the correct re-injection point (before the granulator, best answer is the Mixer) because Formula X transitions from liquid to solid in the granulator. Re-injecting after granulator keeps rejects at reject size. Then calculate yield from recycling 150kg reject pile through granulator (80%) and screens (80%). Note scrubber capacity constraint: at 3 batches/day with 2 scrubber cycles, only 100kg additional capacity exists; each recycled reject pile adds 36kg waste so two recycle runs fit but a third requires a 3rd scrubber cycle causing a net loss.

math.setup: Per batch reject pile = 150kg. Re-inject at Mixer. Track mass through granulator and screens. Check scrubber capacity. Calculate incremental revenue.
steps: Re-inject 150kg at Mixer: through Granulator 150kg*80%=120kg; waste 30kg
Through Screens: 120kg*80%=96kg final product; waste 120kg*5%=6kg unusable; reject 120kg*15%=18kg
Additional waste to scrubber per recycle batch: 30kg + 6kg = 36kg (new reject of 18kg goes back as another potential recycle or scrubber)
For simplicity, treat rejects of rejects as going to scrubber: 36kg waste per recycle run

At 3 batches/day + 2 scrubber cycles: daily waste capacity used = 1350kg out of 2000kg (2 cycles * 1000kg threshold each, but must run at 500kg increments); remaining capacity before 3rd cycle triggered = 2000-1350 = 650kg... re-check: 2 cycles handle up to 1000kg (1 cycle per 500kg); with 1350kg waste, 2 cycles needed; scrubber capacity at 2 cycles = up to ~1000kg cleaned; 1350kg < next threshold of 1500kg so still 2 cycles
Two recycle runs per day add 2*36kg=72kg waste; total 1350+72=1422kg still under 1500kg threshold -> 2 scrubber cycles still sufficient

Third recycle run would add another 36kg: 1422+36=1458kg still under 1500kg; BUT the problem states additional capacity is only 100kg and a 3rd reject pile results in a 3rd scrubber cycle and net incremental loss of $800
Incremental revenue per recycle run: 96kg * $200/kg = $19,200 per batch
Two recycle runs per day: 2 * $19,200 = $38,400/day
Starting from break-even at 3 batches: new daily profit = $0 + $38,400 = $38,400/day
math.answer: Reject recycle can be operated twice per day and must be inserted before the granulator (best: Mixer). This generates $19,200 per recycle batch, and with two recycles per day, Formula X nets $38,400/day.

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm ways to increase profitability of Formula X.

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Run three batches per day to improve fixed cost absorption
Recycle size-rejected pellets from screens back into the process
Increase operational efficiency by reducing misc/labor costs
Reduce scrubber cost through operational changes

categories.name: Supplier
ideas: Renegotiate supplier pricing at contract renewal
Buy ingredients in bulk to obtain volume discounts
Source ingredients with lower unusable content to reduce waste

categories.name: Buyer / Revenue
ideas: Renegotiate buyer pricing upward at contract renewal
Adjust target market or crop segment
Invest in advertising to grow demand
Explore licensing the Formula X patent to other producers

recommendation: Run three batches per day to move from -$10,000/day to break-even, leveraging the fact that the scrubber still only needs two cycles with three batches
Introduce recycling of size-rejected pellets by re-injecting at the Mixer (before the granulator) to recover 96kg of sellable product per recycle run, generating an additional $38,400/day profit
risks: Supplier may not have sufficient ingredients to support a third batch
Buyers under current contracts may not absorb the increased volume
Running 24 hours per day leaves no time for necessary maintenance shutdowns
Patent expires in 10 years, at which point competitive pressure will intensify
Fungi may develop resistance to Formula X over time, reducing product effectiveness
Capital investment required for recycling infrastructure is significant
next_steps: Hire additional personnel to staff the third shift for the third batch
Contact buyers and suppliers to confirm adequate purchase and sale capacity
Request quotes for retrofitting the plant with reject recycling equipment
Monitor scrubber capacity utilization closely as volumes increase
